summary: Design a class that answers who was leading the election at any time t, with ties going to the most recent vote.
mainInsight: Scan the votes once and store the leader after each vote; a query then binary searches the vote times for the last vote at or before t.
invariant: After processing vote i, leaders[i] is the leader of the first i + 1 votes under the tie rule.
canonicalApproach: Precomputed leaders plus binary search on times

personalSolution.notes: Optimal. A leaders list parallel to times removes the dictionary and the key variable (and the defaultdict's silent 0 default).

canonicalCode:
from bisect import bisect_right
from collections import defaultdict


class TopVotedCandidate:
    def __init__(self, persons: list[int], times: list[int]):
        self.times = times
        self.leaders = []                  # leaders[i] = leader right after vote i
        count = defaultdict(int)
        lead = persons[0]
        for p in persons:                  # O(n) preprocessing
            count[p] += 1
            if count[p] >= count[lead]:    # >= because ties go to the most recent vote
                lead = p
            self.leaders.append(lead)

    def q(self, t: int) -> int:
        i = bisect_right(self.times, t) - 1    # last vote with time <= t, O(log n)
        return self.leaders[i]
commonMistakes: Using > instead of >=, which gives ties to the older vote.
Using bisect_left, which skips a vote cast exactly at t.
edgeCases: Query exactly at a vote time.
Ties after the most recent vote.

promptVariants: Why can the leader be computed once, before any query arrives?
What does a query q(t) reduce to?
cards.answer: The leader at time t depends only on the votes up to t, and votes are given in increasing time order. So we can scan the votes once, keep running counts and record the leader after each vote. A query then only needs the index of the last vote with time <= t, found with a binary search on times, and returns the stored leader.
keyPoints: Leader depends on votes up to t
One pass records leader after each vote
Query = binary search for last time <= t
cards.explanation: Trading preprocessing for fast queries is the standard design move.

promptVariants: Why does the preprocessing compare count[p] >= count[lead] instead of >?
What does >= implement in the leader update?
options: The candidate who just voted ties the leader and wins as the latest vote
The candidate who just voted must be ahead of every other candidate
The previous leader keeps the lead on ties because it got there first

cards.answer: The candidate who just voted ties the leader and wins as the latest vote
cards.explanation: count[p] was just incremented, so equality means p has just tied with the leader. The statement gives such ties to the most recent vote, so p becomes the leader.

incorrectOptionExplanations.The candidate who just voted must be ahe: That describes strict >, which would keep the old leader on ties.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The previous leader keeps the lead on ti: The statement's rule is the opposite: the latest vote wins ties.
incorrectOptionExplanations.It avoids updating the leader when two c: Counts start at one for the voting candidate, so zero ties do not arise.

promptVariants: For persons = [0, 1] and times = [3, 7], q(7) must return 1. Which lookup returns the wrong leader?
Votes cast at time t count toward the query. Which index computation violates that rule?
cards.explanation: bisect_left returns the index of the vote at time t itself, and subtracting 1 skips it, so q(7) would read the leader after the first vote (0).

incorrectOptionExplanations.bisect_right(times, t) - 1: bisect_right passes over equal times, so the vote at exactly t is included.
incorrectOptionExplanations.bisect_left(times, t + 1) - 1: For integer times this is equivalent to bisect_right(times, t) - 1.
incorrectOptionExplanations.bisect_right(times, t, 0, len(times)) -: Same as bisect_right over the whole list; correct.

promptVariants: Your solution keeps a dictionary from vote time to leader. What simpler structure can replace it?
How can the lookup of the leader after the binary search be simplified?
cards.answer: Store the leaders in a list parallel to times. bisect_right(times, t) - 1 is an index into both lists, so no dictionary and no separate key variable are needed. It also avoids the default-value trap of a defaultdict returning 0 for an unseen key.
keyPoints: Parallel list indexed by the vote position
Binary search result is an index
cards.explanation: Searching for an index rather than a value keeps the data layout simple.
